Solutions for Questions 1 and 2 will be available after Monday, November 2, 2026. No solution will be provided for Question 3.

Use the RLT package for Questions 1 and 2: RLT in R or rlt in Python. The node-size parameter is nmin in R and min_samples_leaf in Python; both stop splitting a node when it contains at most that many observations. The candidate-predictor parameter is mtry in both languages. Use ordinary random forests, with reinforcement turned off.

Question 1: Bias-variance trade-off simulation

Two important tuning parameters of random forests are node size and mtry. We have performed some preliminary analysis in class. The goal of this question is to perform a larger simulation study for these two tuning parameters.

Consider a regression model with five jointly normally distributed predictors. Each predictor has mean 0 and variance 1, and the correlation between any two different predictors is 0.3. The response is

Y=X1+X3+X5+ε,ε∼N(0,1), Y=X_1+X_3+X_5+\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1),

where the noise is independent of the predictors. Thus the true regression function is f(𝒙)=x1+x3+x5f(\mathbf{x})=x_1+x_3+x_5.

  1. Set up a simulation study with 100 repetitions. Generate 200 test predictor vectors once and keep them fixed. In each repetition, generate 200 new training observations and use the same training data for all tuning settings. Fit 500-tree forests, drawing 200 observations with replacement for each tree. Make the following two comparisons:

    • Fix mtry at 3 and vary node size over 1,5,10,20,301,5,10,20,30.
    • Fix node size at 10 and vary mtry over 1,2,3,4,51,2,3,4,5.

    Leave all other fitting parameters at their defaults. Record the predictions at each test point across repetitions. For each setting, estimate the squared bias and variance at each test point, then average them over the 200 test points. Compare predictions with f(𝒙)f(\mathbf{x}) when estimating bias. Produce two figures, one for each tuning parameter, showing the averaged squared bias and variance. Set a random seed and report it.

Answer:

I use RLT ordinary regression forests and random seed 43210.

For setting ss, let f̂rs(𝒙j)\widehat f_{rs}(\mathbf{x}_j) be the prediction in repetition rr, and let f¯s(𝒙j)\overline f_s(\mathbf{x}_j) be its mean over the 100 repetitions. I calculate

Bias⁡2̂s=1200∑j=1200[f¯s(𝒙j)−f(𝒙j)]2,Var̂s=1200∑j=1200199∑r=1100[f̂rs(𝒙j)−f¯s(𝒙j)]2. \widehat{\operatorname{Bias}^2}_s =\frac{1}{200}\sum_{j=1}^{200} \left[\overline f_s(\mathbf{x}_j)-f(\mathbf{x}_j)\right]^2, \qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_s =\frac{1}{200}\sum_{j=1}^{200} \frac{1}{99}\sum_{r=1}^{100} \left[\widehat f_{rs}(\mathbf{x}_j)-\overline f_s(\mathbf{x}_j)\right]^2.

Thus bias is measured against the true regression function, without adding test-response noise, and variance is the sample variance across repetitions. The squared-bias estimate is the usual plug-in estimate from the finite simulation.

# If needed, install the current RLT package with:
# install.packages("RLT", repos = c("https://teazrq.r-universe.dev",
#                                  "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
library(RLT)
set.seed(43210)

B <- 100L
n_train <- 200L
n_test <- 200L
p <- 5L
Sigma <- matrix(0.3, p, p)
diag(Sigma) <- 1
L <- chol(Sigma)
draw_x <- function(n) matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p) %*% L
truth <- function(x) rowSums(x[, c(1, 3, 5), drop = FALSE])

x_test <- draw_x(n_test)
f_test <- truth(x_test)

# Generate all data before fitting so forest randomness cannot change them.
training <- lapply(seq_len(B), function(r) {
  x <- draw_x(n_train)
  list(x = x, y = truth(x) + rnorm(n_train))
})
forest_seeds <- sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, B)

# (nmin = 10, mtry = 3) appears in both comparisons; fit it once.
settings <- unique(rbind(
  data.frame(nmin = c(1L, 5L, 10L, 20L, 30L), mtry = 3L),
  data.frame(nmin = 10L, mtry = 1:5)
))
rownames(settings) <- NULL
predictions <- array(NA_real_, dim = c(n_test, B, nrow(settings)))

for (r in seq_len(B)) {
  for (s in seq_len(nrow(settings))) {
    forest <- RLT(
      training[[r]]$x, training[[r]]$y,
      model = "regression", ntrees = 500,
      mtry = settings$mtry[s], nmin = settings$nmin[s],
      resample.replace = TRUE, resample.prob = 1,
      reinforcement = FALSE, seed = forest_seeds[r]
    )
    predictions[, r, s] <- as.numeric(predict(forest, x_test)$Prediction)
  }
}

stopifnot(identical(dim(predictions), c(n_test, B, nrow(settings))),
          all(is.finite(predictions)))
pointwise_mean <- apply(predictions, c(1, 3), mean)
pointwise_bias2 <- (pointwise_mean - f_test)^2
pointwise_variance <- apply(predictions, c(1, 3), var)
results <- transform(
  settings,
  squared_bias = colMeans(pointwise_bias2),
  variance = colMeans(pointwise_variance)
)

# Retain the predictions at every test point for every repetition/setting.
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(list(
  seed = 43210, RLT_version = as.character(packageVersion("RLT")),
  x_test = x_test, f_test = f_test, training = training,
  forest_seeds = forest_seeds, settings = settings,
  predictions = predictions, pointwise_bias2 = pointwise_bias2,
  pointwise_variance = pointwise_variance, results = results
), "results/q1a-simulation.rds")
write.csv(results, "results/q1a-summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The shared setting (nmin = 10, mtry = 3) uses the same fitted forests in both comparisons. This requires 900 forests in total. I also use the same forest seed across settings within each repetition to make the comparison reproducible. The RLT version used is 6.1.1.

  1. Discuss your results in terms of the bias-variance trade-off:

    • How does a large node size, such as 30, affect the fit in this example?
    • What are the benefits and drawbacks of using a large mtry value?
    • If each tree instead sampled 100 observations with replacement, would you expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller or larger values? Explain your reasoning. You may use an additional simulation to help, but a particular pattern is not guaranteed.

Answer:

  • A large node size, such as 30, stops splitting earlier and produces simpler trees. In my results, it lowers variance but increases squared bias enough to make the overall fit worse, suggesting underfitting.

  • A larger mtry gives each split more chances to use a useful predictor, which reduces bias. However, the trees can become more similar, limiting the benefit of averaging. In my results, larger mtry lowers squared bias but raises variance.

  • With only 100 bootstrap draws per tree, I would expect a smaller preferred node size, since the same large threshold would stop splitting earlier and produce a coarser fit. However, fewer observations also increase variability, so this shift is not guaranteed.

Question 2: Tuning random forests for MNIST

Use mnist-first2000.csv.gz from the combined ZIP. It contains 2,000 MNIST observations, with the digit label Digit and 784 pixel values.

  • From the first 1,000 observations, keep digits 1, 6, and 7 as the training data. From the remaining 1,000 observations, keep the same digits as the test data.
  • Fit PCA to the training pixels, centering but not scaling them. Use the first 20 principal components as predictors, and project the test observations using the same training means and loadings.

Complete the following tasks using RLT classification forests with 1,000 trees. For each tree, draw a bootstrap sample of the same size as the training set.

  1. Fit a random forest with the default mtry and node-size settings. Report the out-of-bag (OOB) misclassification rate.

Answer:

I use seed 432102.

q2_seed <- 432102L
set.seed(q2_seed)
mnist <- read.csv(gzfile("data/mnist-first2000.csv.gz"))
stopifnot(nrow(mnist) == 2000L, ncol(mnist) == 785L)
q2_digits <- c(1, 6, 7)
q2_first_half <- mnist[1:1000, ]
q2_train_rows <- which(q2_first_half$Digit %in% q2_digits)
q2_train <- q2_first_half[q2_train_rows, ]
q2_y_train <- factor(q2_train$Digit, levels = q2_digits)
q2_pixels <- as.matrix(q2_train[, -1])

q2_pca <- prcomp(q2_pixels, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE, rank. = 20)
q2_x_train <- q2_pca$x[, 1:20, drop = FALSE]

# Omit mtry and nmin to use the installed RLT defaults.
# Also calculate OOB permutation importance for possible reuse in part (b).
q2_default <- RLT(
  q2_x_train, q2_y_train, model = "classification", ntrees = 1000,
  resample.replace = TRUE, resample.prob = 1,
  reinforcement = FALSE, importance = TRUE, seed = q2_seed
)
q2_default_errors <- sum(q2_default$Prediction != q2_y_train)
q2_default_oob <- q2_default_errors / length(q2_y_train)

There are 327 training observations. With 20 predictors, RLT’s defaults are mtry = 10 and node size = 5. The OOB misclassification rate is 4.28% (14 / 327).

  1. Construct a grid of mtry and node-size values to tune the model. Select the setting using OOB misclassification rate. Report the OOB error for each setting and the selected values. Calculate and present the selected forest’s OOB permutation variable importance for the 20 principal components. Comment on your results.

Answer:

I compare mtry values 2, 4, 6, 10, 20 and node sizes 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, giving 25 settings. I select the lowest OOB misclassification rate, breaking exact ties by smaller mtry, then larger node size. I use the same forest seed for each setting.

q2_grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2L, 4L, 6L, 10L, 20L),
                       nmin = c(1L, 3L, 5L, 10L, 20L))
q2_grid <- q2_grid[order(q2_grid$mtry, -q2_grid$nmin), ]
rownames(q2_grid) <- NULL
q2_grid$oob_errors <- NA_integer_
q2_grid$oob_rate <- NA_real_
q2_best_errors <- Inf

for (i in seq_len(nrow(q2_grid))) {
  if (q2_grid$mtry[i] == q2_default$parameters$mtry &&
      q2_grid$nmin[i] == q2_default$parameters$nmin) {
    candidate <- q2_default
  } else {
    candidate <- RLT(
      q2_x_train, q2_y_train, model = "classification", ntrees = 1000,
      mtry = q2_grid$mtry[i], nmin = q2_grid$nmin[i],
      resample.replace = TRUE, resample.prob = 1,
      reinforcement = FALSE, importance = TRUE, seed = q2_seed
    )
  }
  q2_grid$oob_errors[i] <- sum(candidate$Prediction != q2_y_train)
  q2_grid$oob_rate[i] <- q2_grid$oob_errors[i] / length(q2_y_train)
  if (q2_grid$oob_errors[i] < q2_best_errors) {
    q2_best <- candidate
    q2_best_index <- i
    q2_best_errors <- q2_grid$oob_errors[i]
  }
}

q2_selected <- q2_grid[q2_best_index, ]
q2_vi <- data.frame(PC = colnames(q2_x_train),
                    Importance = as.numeric(q2_best$VarImp))
q2_top_pcs <- q2_vi$PC[order(q2_vi$Importance, decreasing = TRUE)][1:3]
dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(q2_grid, "results/q2-oob-grid.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(q2_vi, "results/q2-permutation-importance.csv", row.names = FALSE)

The selected setting is mtry = 2, node size = 10, with OOB error 2.75% (9 / 327).

This improves on the default forest’s OOB error. Considering fewer PCs at each split worked well in this example.

I use RLT’s built-in OOB permutation importance (importance = TRUE). Larger values indicate more loss of predictive performance when that PC is shuffled among OOB observations.

  1. Apply the selected model to the test data and report the misclassification rate and confusion matrix. Use the test labels only for this final assessment.

Answer:

After selecting the model, I keep digits 1, 6, and 7 from rows 1,001–2,000. I project their pixels using the training PCA means and loadings, then apply the selected forest.

q2_second_half <- mnist[1001:2000, ]
q2_test_rows <- 1000L + which(q2_second_half$Digit %in% q2_digits)
q2_test <- mnist[q2_test_rows, ]
q2_x_test <- predict(q2_pca, newdata = as.matrix(q2_test[, -1]))[
  , 1:20, drop = FALSE
]
q2_prediction <- predict(q2_best, q2_x_test)$Prediction
q2_y_test <- factor(q2_test$Digit, levels = q2_digits)
q2_prediction <- factor(q2_prediction, levels = q2_digits)
q2_confusion <- table(Actual = q2_y_test, Predicted = q2_prediction)
q2_test_errors <- sum(q2_prediction != q2_y_test)
q2_test_rate <- q2_test_errors / length(q2_y_test)

write.csv(as.data.frame.matrix(q2_confusion), "results/q2-test-confusion.csv")
saveRDS(list(
  seed = q2_seed, RLT_version = as.character(packageVersion("RLT")),
  train_rows = q2_train_rows, test_rows = q2_test_rows, pca = q2_pca,
  default_oob = q2_default_oob, grid = q2_grid, selected = q2_selected,
  forest = q2_best, importance = q2_vi,
  test_labels = q2_y_test, test_predictions = q2_prediction,
  confusion = q2_confusion, test_rate = q2_test_rate
), "results/q2-analysis.rds")

The test misclassification rate is 2.21% (7 / 317). The confusion matrix has actual digits in rows and predicted digits in columns.

Question 3: Planning a random-forest analysis skill

In earlier homework, some students wrote long skill files with detailed instructions, while others wrote short skills emphasizing their specific requirements or references. These approaches may perform differently depending on the AI and the task. A capable AI may already know standard ways to perform an analysis, so some instructions may be redundant, add little value, or sometimes make the analysis worse. It may be more useful to specify your personal choices for the analysis. An AI with more limited knowledge may benefit from detailed instructions that remind it of the steps to perform.

  1. Write one paragraph describing how you would write a skill that directs an AI to perform a random-forest analysis and produce a report for a future dataset. Discuss how you would balance standard analysis instructions with your personal preferences, considering the AI’s capabilities.

Answer:

I would keep the skill short, covering essential checks and my reporting preferences. For a capable AI, I would emphasize choices such as tuning criteria, figures, and writing style. For a less experienced AI, I would add more detailed analysis steps. I would avoid unnecessary instructions that could distract from the task.

  1. Provide 10 instructions you would consider including in the skill, ordered from the most basic instructions to the more personal preferences. Your list may cover computation, tuning, tables, figures, interpretation, presentation, or other aspects of a random-forest report.

Answer:

  1. Identify the outcome and whether the task is regression or classification.
  2. Check variable types, missing values, and invalid entries.
  3. Reserve a test set for final evaluation.
  4. Learn preprocessing steps from training data only.
  5. Set a random seed and record model settings.
  6. Fit forests and tune using training OOB error or cross-validation.
  7. Evaluate the selected model on the test set using appropriate metrics.
  8. Show permutation importance for the most useful predictors.
  9. Use small tables and clearly labeled figures.
  10. Keep the report concise and explain the main findings in plain language.

You only need to discuss how the skill should be written. You are not required to write a complete skill file or test it.
